name: Money illusion
statement: People judge money by its face value, so identical real outcomes look better when the numbers are bigger, and nominal prices resist coming down.
meaning: Two definitions travel under this name. Irving Fisher's is a failure of perception: people do not notice that the unit of money itself changes in value, so a mark or a dollar feels fixed while goods appear to move. The experimental literature uses a narrower test. Money illusion is present when behaviour differs across two situations that are identical in real terms and differ only in how the numbers are written. That makes it a framing effect, and it is measurable, which is why nearly all the evidence since 1997 is built on it. The evidence comes in three kinds that are usually quoted together and should not be. Survey vignettes ask people to judge hypothetical raises, house sales and contracts. Laboratory pricing games pay real money for getting the arithmetic right. Field data record what wages and house prices actually did. The three do not agree about how much illusion there is. The laboratory results also turn on a mechanism the vignettes cannot show, which is what players expect other players to do.

origin.where: The Money Illusion (Adelphi Company, New York)
origin.note: The book grew out of lectures given in the summer of 1927 at the Geneva School of International Studies. Fisher defines the illusion in its first chapter as "the failure to perceive that the dollar, or any other unit of money, expands or shrinks in value", and his evidence is anecdote rather than measurement. The experimental literature dates instead from Shafir, Diamond and Tversky's 1997 paper in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, which recast the term as a framing effect and supplied the survey problems used ever since.

evidence: Fisher's case was a travelogue. Touring Germany in 1922 with Frederick W. Roman, he talked at length with twenty-four men and women met by chance, and only one of them had any idea that the mark had changed in value. A shopkeeper on the outskirts of Berlin told him the shirt she had just sold him would cost as much to replace as she had charged, and then said she had made a profit on it because she had bought it for less. By then, Fisher writes, the mark had depreciated by more than ninety-eight per cent. Shafir, Diamond and Tversky replaced the anecdotes with four survey problems, whose original figures are quoted here from the tables of Ziano and colleagues' replication rather than from the 1997 paper, which could not be obtained. Asked about Ann, who got a 2% raise with no inflation, and Barbara, who got a 5% raise with 4% inflation, 71% of 150 respondents said Ann was doing better in economic terms, but only 36% of 69 thought her happier and 65% of 139 thought her more likely to leave her job. Ranking three men who bought and sold a house, 47% put first the seller with a 23% nominal gain and a 2% real loss, and 54% put last the seller with a 23% nominal loss and a 2% real gain. Told that all prices and salaries had risen 25%, 38% said they were less likely to buy an armchair and 43% said they were more likely to sell one. Offered two sale contracts, 81% of 47 chose the one that was riskless in real terms when the choice was described in real terms, against 59% of 49 in nominal terms and 54% of 43 in neutral terms. Fehr and Tyran took the question into a paid pricing game with 130 subjects at the University of Zurich. A fully anticipated monetary shock moved the average equilibrium price from 18 to 6. Against computers that best-replied, subjects seeing real payoffs adjusted at once, and subjects seeing nominal payoffs mostly did too, with 80% fully adjusting and the average price 2.1 units too high. Against other humans the gap was far larger. Average prices stood 3.1 units above equilibrium in the first period after the shock under the real frame and 7.1 units above it under the nominal frame, and the nominal groups took eight periods to fall to the real frame's opening deviation. Prices were significantly out of equilibrium for 12 periods under the nominal frame and 2 under the real one. Nominal groups lost 26% of their potential payoff over the first ten post-shock periods, against slightly under 14% for real groups. A further 96 subjects faced a positive shock instead, and the nominal groups were out of equilibrium for only three periods.

replication.headline: All four survey problems replicated at N = 604, but a redesigned re-run of the strongest laboratory experiment found no first-order money illusion at all.
replication.detail: Ziano, Li, Tsun, Lei, Kamath, Cheng and Feldman ran all four Shafir problems on 604 MTurk workers and called every one a success. Problem 1 gave Cramer's V of 0.28, 95% CI [0.21, 0.36], against 0.26 [0.17, 0.37] recalculated by them from the original. In problem 2 the seller with the largest nominal gain was ranked first by 70% against 47% originally. In problem 3 the buy and sell splits were 6/47/47 and 43/49/8 per cent against 7/55/38 and 43/42/15. Problem 4 gave V = 0.17 [0.10, 0.25] against 0.25 [0.13, 0.42]. De Moraes Ferreira and colleagues then put the four problems to a Brazilian sample. Of the 446 people who started the questionnaire, 372 finished at least one problem and were analysed. The patterns held, with 78% of the 112 asked in economic terms naming the person whose raise was larger in real terms as better off, and 43% of 269 ranking the largest nominal gain first. The laboratory side went the other way. Petersen and Winn rebuilt Fehr and Tyran's game for 225 subjects at Chapman University and the University of California, Santa Cruz, changing three things: a nominal payoff mapping under which the illusion-driven choice and the rational choice differ, a marked focal point present in both frames, and best-reply functions that are symmetric across positive and negative shocks. Not a single decision in their computerised nominal treatment was consistent with taking nominal payoffs for real ones. What remained they attribute to the difficulty of finding the equilibrium among 1,800 payoffs, plus a weak preference for high nominal payoffs among prices that already maximise real payoffs. Their focal point did not shrink the opening deviation in the nominal human treatment, which at 5.6 units was not significantly different from Fehr and Tyran's 7.1, but it cut the duration of inertia by 42%. Fehr and Tyran replied in the same issue that both datasets show money illusion driving expectations after a negative shock, and that Petersen and Winn misread their own data.

study.cite: Ziano, I., Li, J., Tsun, S. M., Lei, H. C., Kamath, A. A., Cheng, B. L., & Feldman, G. (2021). Revisiting "money illusion": Replication and extension of Shafir, Diamond, and Tversky (1997). Journal of Economic Psychology, 83, 102349.

limits: The survey effect is not uniform across its four problems. In the replication the economic-terms condition of problem 1 fell from 71% to 56% and no longer differed from chance, p = .14, and the authors called the replication successful on the overall pattern rather than on that cell. Problem 4 is thinner still. Its original cells held 47, 49 and 43 respondents, and in the replication only the real-terms frame differed from an even split, with p = .16 for the nominal frame and p = .73 for the neutral one. The effect there lives in the contrast between conditions, not in any one of them. The Cramer's V figures attributed to the original study carry the replication's own footnote marking them as recalculated. The vignettes are hypothetical and pay nothing for a correct answer, which is the contrast Ziano and colleagues draw with the incentivised laboratory work. The neuroimaging evidence is smaller than its title suggests. Weber, Rangel, Wibral and Falk scanned 24 subjects who earned money in a dot-estimation task under two catalogues whose prices and incomes differed by 50%, leaving purchasing power identical. Two subjects were dropped for scanner dysfunction and four for head movement. The ventromedial prefrontal contrast at 12/47/0 was reported at p < 0.001 uncorrected with a 10-voxel extent threshold, and the correlation with a questionnaire measure of illusion, Spearman's r = 0.60, p < 0.01, is a cross-subject correlation in that reduced sample. The authors state plainly that their experiment produced no behavioural difference. On the field side, Grigsby, Hurst and Yildirmaz's payroll records from 2008 to 2016 show that 2.5% of workers who stayed in the same job took a cut in nominal base pay in a given year, and that 32% of hourly and 35% of salaried stayers saw no change at all. That is rigidity, and it says nothing about the cause. About 27% of job-changers took a cut on switching, so the aggregate economy is more flexible than the stayer figure alone implies. Those are the published article's figures; the 2019 working paper gave 2.4% for stayers, 38% for job-changers and 9% for the two groups pooled. Brunnermeier and Julliard's housing evidence is a time-series decomposition of the United Kingdom price-rent ratio from 1966:Q2 to 2004:Q4, in which inflation explains much of an estimated mispricing component; no individual is measured. On whether money illusion behaves differently where inflation is high, the only thing located was the Brazilian replication succeeding. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and the open web on 21 September 2026 for experimental work in high-inflation economies turned up nothing usable.
misreadings: The strongest laboratory finding is not that individuals stay confused. Fehr and Tyran's second experiment, a coordination game with 174 students and three ranked equilibria, shows the opposite at the individual level. Playing against computers under the nominal frame, the share choosing the efficient equilibrium rose from 22.7% in period 1 to 81.8% by period 30, so individual illusion faded with practice. Playing against other humans under the same frame, not one subject chose that equilibrium in any of the 30 periods, and 84% had settled on the equilibrium with the highest nominal payoff and a lower real one by the end. Under the real frame 98% played the efficient equilibrium in the final four periods. The lasting effect runs through beliefs about what others will do, not through arithmetic that people cannot perform. A second misreading treats the effect as symmetric. In the price-setting experiment nominal groups were out of equilibrium for 12 periods after a negative shock and three after a positive one, and Noussair, Richter and Tyran report the same asymmetry in an experimental asset market. Money illusion in this literature is a claim about resistance to nominal cuts. Third, downward nominal wage rigidity is evidence that wages rarely fall, not evidence of why. Fourth, the headline that the brain exhibits money illusion describes a between-condition contrast at an uncorrected threshold in a study whose subjects behaved identically in the two conditions. Finally, Fisher's illusion and the experimental one are different claims. Fisher's shopkeeper did not know the unit had moved. A subject in a framing experiment is told the inflation rate and still answers differently depending on how the numbers are laid out.

sources.text: Fisher, I. (1928). The Money Illusion. New York: Adelphi Company. Read in full from the scanned copy at the Internet Archive; the definition, the twenty-four German travellers and the Berlin shopkeeper are in chapter I.

Shafir, E., Diamond, P., & Tversky, A. (1997). Money Illusion. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 112(2), 341-374. Bibliographic record read at Crossref, which gives no abstract. The article itself was not obtained on 21 September 2026. Oxford Academic returned a Cloudflare bot challenge to a direct request and only journal navigation to a rendering fetch, and the full-text link Crossref deposits for similarity checking returned the same challenge. Unpaywall and OpenAlex both record it as closed with no repository copy, Semantic Scholar holds no record under this DOI, MIT's and Princeton's repositories hold no file, and the reprint in Choices, Values, and Frames at the Internet Archive is lending-restricted and refused download. The survey figures are quoted here from the tables of Ziano and colleagues (2021).

Fehr, E., & Tyran, J.-R. (2001). Does Money Illusion Matter? American Economic Review, 91(5), 1239-1262. Read in full from the copy hosted by the University of Zurich; the price paths, deviations and efficiency losses come from its Tables 3 and 4 and section III.

Fehr, E., & Tyran, J.-R. (2007). Money illusion and coordination failure. Games and Economic Behavior, 58(2), 246-268. The coordination-game figures on this page are read from the earlier CESifo Working Paper 1141 of February 2004, which was obtained in full. The published version was not obtained on 21 September 2026: Elsevier refused the article page, Crossref deposits no abstract for it, and the only repository copy OpenAlex lists, at the Zurich Open Repository, sits behind a proof-of-work bot challenge.

Fehr, E., & Tyran, J.-R. (2008). Limited Rationality and Strategic Interaction: The Impact of the Strategic Environment on Nominal Inertia. Econometrica, 76(2), 353-394. The article was not obtained on 21 September 2026, and no figure from it appears on this page. Wiley refused the article page. The open copy that Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex point to is not the article: it is the SSRN working-paper record, and SSRN returned a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall. The University of Zurich's IEW working paper 130 and the Zurich Open Repository copy sit behind an Anubis proof-of-work challenge that cannot be cleared from a rotating address, which is again a bot challenge and not a paywall. The Copenhagen research portal record holds no file. The citation was confirmed at Crossref and at the Econometric Society.

Ziano, I., Li, J., Tsun, S. M., Lei, H. C., Kamath, A. A., Cheng, B. L., & Feldman, G. (2021). Revisiting "money illusion": Replication and extension of Shafir, Diamond, and Tversky (1997). Journal of Economic Psychology, 83, 102349. Read in full from the authors' preprint on OSF; the original and replication figures come from its Tables 3, 5, 7 and 9. The published version was not obtained, Elsevier having refused the article page on 21 September 2026. The preprint's abstract gives the original Problem 2 share as 48% where its own results section gives 47%; the 47% is used here.

de Moraes Ferreira, M., Yumi Tsushima Santiago, M., Bastos, R., Fatori, D., Sardinha Borborema, R., Seda, L., & Camargo Batistuzzo, M. (2024). Replication: The money illusion effect in a Brazilian sample and meta-analyses. Journal of Economic Psychology, 104, 102744. The Brazilian figures here are read from the authors' preprint of 20 December 2023, downloaded in full from OSF, which is titled for the replication alone and whose text nowhere uses the word meta-analysis. The published version was not obtained: Elsevier refused the article page on 21 September 2026 and Crossref deposits no abstract for it.

Petersen, L., & Winn, A. (2014). Does Money Illusion Matter? Comment. American Economic Review, 104(3), 1047-1062. Read in full from the authors' working-paper version, titled "The Role of Money Illusion in Nominal Price Adjustment". The published article is gated behind American Economic Association membership or purchase, which is a paywall rather than a bot challenge. Its published abstract, read at the association on 21 September 2026, is word for word the working paper's, so the two agree on what the paper claims.

Fehr, E., & Tyran, J.-R. (2014). Does Money Illusion Matter? Reply. American Economic Review, 104(3), 1063-1071. The published abstract was read at the American Economic Association on 21 September 2026, and the reply's online appendix was obtained in full from the association's asset server. The reply's own text was not obtained: the association gates the PDF behind membership or purchase, which is a paywall rather than a bot challenge, and the Zurich Open Repository copy sits behind a proof-of-work challenge. The green open-access copy that OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar all list for this DOI is that online appendix, not the article.

Weber, B., Rangel, A., Wibral, M., & Falk, A. (2009). The medial prefrontal cortex exhibits money illusion. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 106(13), 5025-5028. Read in full from the open copy at Europe PMC.

Grigsby, J., Hurst, E., & Yildirmaz, A. (2021). Aggregate Nominal Wage Adjustments: New Evidence from Administrative Payroll Data. American Economic Review, 111(2), 428-471. The wage figures on this page are the published article's, read from the authors' final submission of 23 August 2020 hosted on Erik Hurst's site, whose abstract matches the abstract the publisher deposited at Crossref. The NBER working paper 25628 of March 2019 was also read in full and differs: 2.4% rather than 2.5% for job-stayers, 38% rather than about 27% for job-changers, and a pooled stayer-and-changer figure of 9% that the later text does not repeat.

Brunnermeier, M. K., & Julliard, C. (2008). Money Illusion and Housing Frenzies. Review of Financial Studies, 21(1), 135-180. The sample period and the mispricing decomposition are read from the NBER working-paper version, number 12810 of December 2006, and confirmed in the separate London School of Economics deposit of July 2006. The published article was not obtained on 21 September 2026: Oxford Academic returned a Cloudflare bot challenge to the open-access PDF that OpenAlex lists for it, which is a bot challenge and not a paywall.

Noussair, C. N., Richter, G., & Tyran, J.-R. (2012). Money Illusion and Nominal Inertia in Experimental Asset Markets. Journal of Behavioral Finance, 13(1), 27-37. Bibliographic record verified at Crossref, which deposits no abstract, and against the Tilburg University research portal, whose record holds no file and whose abstract reports that nominal prices adjust upward rapidly after an inflationary shock with no real effects, while after a deflationary shock they display considerable inertia. The article itself was not obtained on 21 September 2026, with Taylor and Francis refusing the article page, and only that direction of asymmetry is used here.
